title: When should one make the intention to fast for missed Ramadan fasts?
headline: Four schools require the make-up fast's intention before dawn, differing on details

summary.text: The four schools agree that the intention for a make-up (qada) fast must be made during the night before Fajr, since it is an obligatory fast. They differ on how many nights need a fresh intention, whether the year being made up must be specified, and what a day fasted without a night intention counts as.

How do I make an intention for a qadha fast?

paragraphs.text: The verses governing qada are 2:183–185 and 2:187. The obligation is stated in 2:183, the substitute-days concession in 2:184, and the timing of the fast's beginning in 2:187. None of these verses mentions intention explicitly, which is why the schools built the timing of the intention on hadith and on reasoning from the verse's structure.

The Hanafis read 2:187 as marking the night as a time of eating and drinking and the day as the single, continuous act of fasting, so a resolve joined to the greater part of the day suffices; al-Marghinani argues that the fast is one extended pillar, and the intention's function is only to specify it, so it is weighted toward the majority of the day. The other three schools read the same verse as fixing the start of the fast at Fajr, so whatever precedes Fajr belongs to the night and must carry the intention.

The central report is Hafsah's: "Whoever does not firmly resolve to fast before dawn has no fast" (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 730). Tirmidhi states he knows it as a raised report only through Yahya ibn Ayyub, that it is also reported from Nafi' from Ibn Umar as Ibn Umar's own saying, "and that is more authentic," and that it came from al-Zuhri as a halted report. Abu Dawud adds that Ma'mar, al-Zubaydi, Ibn Uyaynah and Yunus al-Ayli all stopped it at Hafsah rather than raising it to the Prophet ﷺ.

Grades differ by edition and grader. On the major published gradings the raised version is marked Sahih by Ahmad Shakir and al-Albani, and Da'if by Zubair Ali Zai, in Tirmidhi 730; Abu Dawud 2454 carries Sahih for al-Albani and Abdul Hamid and Da'if for Zubair Ali Zai; Nasa'i 2331–2332 carries Sahih for Abu Ghuddah and al-Albani and Da'if for Zubair Ali Zai. The Darussalam edition of Tirmidhi marks it Da'if, and al-Albani discussed at length the dispute over raising and stopping it. The stopped versions, where Hafsah speaks in her own words, are graded Sahih Mawquf. Ibn Hajar, as quoted in a contemporary fatwa, noted that al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Tirmidhi and Ibn Abi Hatim judged it mawquf.

Two supporting reports pull the other way. Aisha's hadith, in Sahih Muslim and al-Nasa'i, has the Prophet ﷺ come to her, find no food, and say "Then I am fasting," then later eat when a gift arrived, having begun the day intending a fast. The Ashura reports are stronger still: the Prophet ﷺ sent a man to announce mid-morning that whoever had eaten should complete the day and whoever had not should fast.

The Hanafi school requires the intention before Fajr for qada. Ramadan and a time-specified vow may be intended up to mid-morning, but qada is expressly excluded from that concession and requires tabyit and ta'yin; Ibn Abidin states that qada of Ramadan and of a specified vow requires tabyit and specification. One intention per day is required.

The Maliki school requires the intention before Fajr in all types of fast without distinction between obligatory and voluntary. One intention per day is required for qada; a single intention suffices only for a fast whose continuity is required by law, such as Ramadan. Specifying the year being made up is not required, since a general intention of qada suffices.

The Shafi'i school requires the intention before Fajr for every obligatory fast, qada included; a daytime intention is invalid with no disagreement. One intention per day is required, with specification of what is being fasted. Al-Shirbini cites the Hafsah report and restricts it to obligatory fasts by the evidence of Aisha's report.

The Hanbali school requires the intention before Fajr for qada; any part of the night will do, and eating or intimacy after the intention does not void it. One intention per day is required, and the mashhur position rejects one intention for the month. Ibn Qudama reports a narration from Ahmad that a man who intended the qada of Ramadan during the day without a night intention is not at fault, and he explains it away by saying the intention must have been carried over into a part of the night.

Tirmidhi supplies the harmonisation that most later scholars adopted: the meaning is that there is no valid fast for one who did not resolve before dawn in Ramadan, or in making up a missed Ramadan fast, or in a vowed fast, while for a voluntary fast it is permitted to intend after morning has begun, this being the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq. Ibn Rushd frames it as a choice of method: whoever preferred one report over another took Hafsah's and required the night intention outright, while whoever chose to combine the reports distinguished voluntary from obligatory, reading Hafsah's report as governing the obligatory fast and Aisha's and Mu'awiyah's as governing the voluntary. Al-Shirbini states the harmonisation explicitly, saying the Hafsah report is carried to the obligatory fast by the evidence of Aisha's report.

The Hanafis did not reject the report but re-read its wording. Al-Marghinani says the report is carried on negation of merit and perfection, or its meaning is that he did not intend it as a fast from the night, and he adds that the Ashura command is accounted for because that fast's obligation was later settled, and because the day is one extended act whose intention is weighted by the majority of it. Ibn Qudama answers the Ashura point differently, saying the obligation of Ashura was never firmly established, since Mu'awiyah reported the Prophet ﷺ saying it was not written upon them.

The transmission problem was met by grading. Those who required the night intention pointed to al-Daruqutni's Aisha route with the words "before the rising of dawn," which he declared all its narrators trustworthy, and to the raising by Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr from al-Zuhri, whom Ibn Qudama calls one of the lofty trustworthy narrators. Those who weakened it pointed to the stopping by four of al-Zuhri's students and to Tirmidhi's own statement that Ibn Umar's own saying is more authentic, with al-Albani's extended critique. Even so, the practical outcome among the schools is close: a day fasted for qada without a night intention is treated as a voluntary fast that earns reward, while the obligation to make up the day remains.

Egypt's Dar al-Ifta, in fatwa 8197 of December 2023, fixed the window precisely: tabyit means contracting the intention at night, and its earliest time is sunset and entry into the night of the day to be fasted, so an intention formed before Maghrib does not count. The same body's fatwa on qada states that one may not intend the qada in the morning of the day itself, because specification of the qada is obligatory from the night before Fajr, and a vague intention to fast is not enough. It also held that intending qada without naming the year is valid and sufficient.

IslamQA (2025) answered a woman who had resolved at night but made the resolve conditional and woke unsure: her day counts as a voluntary fast and she still owes the qada, citing al-Nawawi's statement that no obligatory fast, including qada and expiation, is valid with a daytime intention. On multiple days, IslamQA and Shaykh Abd al-Rahman al-Barrak held that a separate intention is required for each day of qada, because Ramadan's continuity is fixed by the Law while qada is not. Ibn Baz likewise held an intention is needed for each day, and that getting up for the pre-dawn meal itself constitutes the intention. Ibn Uthaymeen allowed one intention at the start of Ramadan but required a fresh one after any break in continuity. AMJA's Shaykh Salah al-Sawi required a nightly intention for Ramadan and exempted only voluntary fasts. The Permanent Committee made the night intention obligatory for each day's fast. Hanafi-oriented fatwa services state the qada intention must be made before subh sadiq and that a general intention to fast the next day suffices, without naming today or tomorrow.
